about: Dishes and their ingredients (core and optional), for 'name the ingredients' play. Ingredients and origins are facts read from English Wikipedia and the Wikibooks Cookbook, written in our own words.
attribution: Ingredient facts from English Wikipedia and Wikibooks (CC BY-SA 4.0).

dishes.label: Abgoosht
dishes.origin: Served in the stoneware crock it is named for, it is eaten in two stages: the broth with bread first, then the mashed solids.

dishes.label: Ackee and saltfish
dishes.origin: Jamaica's national dish pairs a fruit from West Africa that is toxic until ripe with salted cod once shipped in for enslaved people.

dishes.label: Adana kebab
dishes.origin: Adana kebab has protected origin status since 2005, and only a vendor who passes a local chamber of commerce inspection can sell the original.

dishes.label: Adobo
dishes.origin: Vinegar keeps it good for days without a fridge, so Filipino travelers pack it; the Spanish name was stuck on a cooking style that was already here.

dishes.label: Æbleskiver
dishes.origin: The name means apple slices, yet modern ones hold no apple; Danes eat them at Christmas with jam, powdered sugar and gløgg.

dishes.label: Ajiaco
dishes.origin: Bogotá's version needs three kinds of potato and a weed the locals call guascas; Cuba and Peru each cook a quite different ajiaco.

dishes.label: Ajoblanco
dishes.origin: Spain's white gazpacho was built on Arab-introduced almonds; Almáchar holds a festival for it each September.

dishes.label: Alfajor
dishes.origin: Born in Moorish Spain, its name comes from the Arabic for luxurious; Argentines now eat over a billion of the dulce de leche sandwiches a year.

dishes.label: Aloo gobi
dishes.origin: Potato and cauliflower in turmeric-yellow spices; it even gets screen time in the film Bend It Like Beckham.

dishes.label: Ambrosia
dishes.origin: A Southern potluck staple named for the food of the Greek gods; its first known mention is in an 1867 Dixie cookbook.

dishes.label: Arancini
dishes.origin: Sicilians eat these 'little oranges' on Saint Lucy's Day, 13 December, when bread and pasta are skipped to remember a 1646 grain ship.

dishes.label: Arepa
dishes.origin: Corn patties were baked on clay slabs around 3,000 years ago; the pre-cooked flour that made them a daily staple was invented in the 1950s.

dishes.label: Arroz chaufa
dishes.origin: Peru's Chinese-immigrant fried rice, born in the chifa kitchens of the late 1800s; the 'aeropuerto' version adds a pile of stir-fried noodles.

dishes.label: Arroz con pollo
dishes.origin: Puerto Ricans insist it needs beer and annatto oil; Spaniards use saffron. It resembles paella and may be a New World cousin of it.

dishes.label: Meat pie
dishes.origin: Aussies eat 270 million a year; a premier once called the footy-match snack Australia's national dish, and pie floaters sink one in pea soup.

dishes.label: Babka
dishes.origin: Bakers rolled leftover challah dough around jam and baked it as a loaf; the chocolate version is a later New York invention.

dishes.label: Bacalhau à Brás
dishes.origin: Born in Lisbon's Bairro Alto in the 1800s, this shredded salt cod scramble is said to be Cristiano Ronaldo's favourite dish.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Salt Cod and Potato Casserole (Bacalhau à Zé do Pipo)

dishes.label: Baingan bharta
dishes.origin: Smoky mashed eggplant; in Maharashtra's harvest season whole villages hold a 'bharit party', and Greenpeace once cooked 342 kg of it in Delhi.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Baingan Bartha (South Indian Eggplant with Coconut and Chili) I

dishes.label: Bak kut teh
dishes.origin: Its name means 'meat bone tea' yet there is no tea in the pot; Malaysia and Singapore still squabble over who invented it.

dishes.label: Baklava
dishes.origin: Ottoman sultans handed trays of it to their Janissary troops in a Ramadan parade, and Greeks, Turks and Armenians still argue over who invented it.

dishes.label: Balti
dishes.origin: Birmingham's Balti Triangle made this curry famous, and cooks there serve it in the thin steel bowl it is named for.

dishes.label: Bananas Foster
dishes.origin: Brennan's in New Orleans made it in 1951 and named it after a local civic leader; waiters still set it ablaze at the table.

dishes.label: Bandeja paisa
dishes.origin: Colombia once weighed making it the national dish, but critics said only one region really eats it.

dishes.label: Bánh mì
dishes.origin: The French brought the baguette in the 1860s; wartime rice flour made it cheap, and Saigon vendors then piled on pickles, herbs and chiles.

dishes.label: Banh xeo
dishes.origin: Named for the sizzle of batter hitting a hot pan; Vietnamese Buddhists sometimes eat it in place of rice on certain lunar days.

dishes.label: Banitsa
dishes.origin: Bulgarians bake lucky charms such as dogwood buds into the New Year's Eve banitsa, then spin the pan so each person gets a fortune.

dishes.label: Banoffee pie
dishes.origin: Born in 1971 at the Hungry Monk restaurant in East Sussex after trials with apple and mandarin; its makers offered £10,000 to anyone who disproved their claim.

dishes.label: Baozi
dishes.origin: Legend says the general Zhuge Liang invented them as stand-ins for human heads in a river sacrifice; from China they spread as siopao, bakpao and nikuman.

dishes.label: Bara brith
dishes.origin: The name means speckled bread, and Welsh settlers carried it to Patagonia in 1865, where it is still baked as torta negra.

dishes.label: Basbousa
dishes.origin: Some say its name means just a kiss in Arabic; its ancestor may be a 9th-century rice sweet from the Abbasid court, later remade with semolina.

dishes.label: Baumkuchen
dishes.origin: Layers of batter browned on a rotating spit leave tree-ring stripes; in Japan it is a popular wedding gift because rings stand for long life.

dishes.label: Beef Stroganoff
dishes.origin: Named after the noble Stroganov family; its first known recipe in 1871 had no onions, no mushrooms and no alcohol.

dishes.label: Beignet
dishes.origin: French settlers brought the fried dough to New Orleans in the 1700s, and Louisiana later made it an official state doughnut.

dishes.label: Berliner
dishes.origin: Fried-dough balls with jam appear in a printed 1485 German cookbook; Kennedy's famous line did not accidentally call himself a doughnut.

dishes.label: Bhel puri
dishes.origin: Mumbai's beach snack; a Mumbai restaurant claims it invented it, and a legend says a warrior king wanted a quick bite for soldiers.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Bhel Puri (Indian Puffed Rice and Vegetable Snack)

dishes.label: Bibimbap
dishes.origin: The name means mixed rice, and one theory says it began as leftovers from ancestral rites tipped into a single bowl.

dishes.label: Bibingka
dishes.origin: Baked between coals over and under, it is the Christmas snack after Simbang Gabi mass; one town baked a kilometre-long cassava one.

dishes.label: Bigos
dishes.origin: Poland's hunter's stew improves with every reheating, and the national epic Pan Tadeusz has a bear-hunt scene built around a pot of it.

dishes.label: Bingsu
dishes.origin: Joseon-era Koreans cooled themselves with ice from royal stone ice houses; condensed milk and syrup arrived after the Korean War.

dishes.label: Birria
dishes.origin: Jalisco's goat stew is served at weddings and funerals alike, and Tijuana's beef version with dipping consomé took the taco world by storm.

dishes.label: Biryani
dishes.origin: Historians still argue whether it was born in Mughal kitchens or came from Persia; in India it is the single most-ordered dish on delivery apps.

dishes.label: Black Forest cake
dishes.origin: The name may come from the region's cherry schnapps; EU rules say the kirsch in a real one must come from Black Forest cherries.

dishes.label: Blancmange
dishes.origin: A medieval 'white dish' of almond milk, sugar and shredded capon, it was invalid food and a Lenten stand-in long before it became a pudding.

dishes.label: Blini
dishes.origin: Eaten twice a day in Maslenitsa, the Russian butter week at winter's end; traditionally baked in a Russian oven.

dishes.label: Boat noodles
dishes.origin: Sold from paddling boats on Bangkok's canals, it still comes in tiny bowls, a trick that kept the boat steady.

dishes.label: Bobotie
dishes.origin: Cape Malay cooks made it from a 1600s Dutch recipe; a Masters champion once served it at Augusta, and Boers took it to Patagonia.

dishes.label: Bœuf bourguignon
dishes.origin: Not really a Burgundian recipe: it is first documented in 1867, and only became a regional specialty in the 20th century.

dishes.label: Börek
dishes.origin: Its name means rolled or twisted, a Persian poet once staged a war between börek and pilaf, and Sephardic Jews eat bourekas at Shabbat breakfast.

dishes.label: Borscht
dishes.origin: It began as a sour soup of pickled hogweed that gave it its Slavic name; beetroot joined later in Ukraine, and tomatoes eventually took over the tang.

dishes.label: Bougatsa
dishes.origin: A Greek breakfast pastry, perhaps descended from an ancient Roman placenta cake; Thessaloniki and Serres claim its modern form.

dishes.label: Bouillabaisse
dishes.origin: Marseille fishermen first made it from bony rockfish they could not sell; in 1980 eleven restaurants signed a charter to define it.

dishes.label: Boxty
dishes.origin: An old rhyme warns that if you cannot make boxty you will never get a man; boiled boxty is a Halloween tradition in the north midlands.

dishes.label: Bratwurst
dishes.origin: Nuremberg's grilling sausages were written up in 1313, and in Wisconsin a whole Memorial Day festival is built around them.

dishes.label: Bread and butter pudding
dishes.origin: It grew out of medieval whitepot, and an early 1728 recipe called for a pound of butter, ten egg yolks and three pints of cream.

dishes.label: Bread pudding
dishes.origin: Eleventh-century English cooks used up stale loaves; the poor man's pudding later gained eggs and milk and went worldwide.

dishes.label: Brunswick stew
dishes.origin: Virginia and Georgia both claim it; a 1941 Virginia guide says a camp cook threw it all in a pot, and the first batch was squirrel.

dishes.label: Bruschetta
dishes.origin: Its name comes from a Roman word for 'toasted over coals', and in Tuscany and Umbria it began as a way to taste the year's first olive oil.

dishes.label: Bubble and squeak
dishes.origin: Named for the sounds it makes in the pan; the first recipes in 1806 were all cabbage and beef, with potatoes joining much later.

dishes.label: Budae jjigae
dishes.origin: Born from the scraps and canned goods near US army bases after the Korean War; Spam was only legal to sell there from 1987.

dishes.label: Buddha Jumps Over the Wall
dishes.origin: A Fujian banquet stew simmered for a day or two in a wine jar; the name says even a vegetarian Buddha would leap a wall for a taste.

dishes.label: Buffalo wings
dishes.origin: Said to be born at Buffalo's Anchor Bar in 1964 when wings meant for stock were fried instead; the city declared Chicken Wing Day in 1977.

dishes.label: Bulgogi
dishes.origin: Its name means 'fire meat'; the dish traces back to ancient Goguryeo skewers called maekjeok, and Joseon nobles later ate it as neobiani.

dishes.label: Bún bò Huế
dishes.origin: Born in the old imperial capital of Huế, its fiery lemongrass broth is cooked in a round-bottomed aluminium pot, and the noodles are thicker than in pho.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Vietnamese Rice Noodle and Beef Soup (Bún bò Huế)

dishes.label: Bun cha
dishes.origin: Hanoi's lunchtime grilled-pork-and-noodles dish, which shot to global fame when Obama and Bourdain ate it there in 2016.

dishes.label: Bún riêu
dishes.origin: A sour, tomato-red Vietnamese soup built on pounded paddy crabs, shell and all, and usually eaten in the heat of summer.

dishes.label: Bunny chow
dishes.origin: Durban's Indian community hollowed out loaves to hold curry for takeaway; locals simply ask for a quarter mutton.

dishes.label: Buñuelo
dishes.origin: First recorded among Spain's Moriscos, buñuelos now bring luck in Latin America and show up at Christmas, Easter and Hanukkah.

dishes.label: Burgoo
dishes.origin: A Kentucky Derby stew once made of squirrel and rabbit; a good one is said to be thick enough to stand a spoon in.

dishes.label: Butter chicken
dishes.origin: Said to be born when Moti Mahal cooks tossed leftover tandoori chicken into a buttery tomato gravy; heirs of the founders still fight over who invented it.

dishes.label: Butter tart
dishes.origin: Canadians still fight over raisins in them; the oldest printed recipe is from Barrie, Ontario around 1900, and Midland holds a festival for them.

dishes.label: Cabbage roll
dishes.origin: Hungarians once called cabbage-and-meat the coat of arms of Hungary; Romania's sarmale are a Christmas must.

dishes.label: Cacciatore
dishes.origin: The name means hunter's style, and Sophia Loren was quoted praising sweet red peppers as the key to a proper chicken version.

dishes.label: Caesar salad
dishes.origin: Caesar Cardini reportedly tossed it together in Tijuana on a busy Fourth of July in 1924; his daughter says the original had no anchovies.

dishes.label: Caldo verde
dishes.origin: Portugal's green broth from the Minho was voted one of the country's Seven Wonders of Gastronomy in 2011.

dishes.label: California roll
dishes.origin: Los Angeles and Vancouver chefs both claim it; it went inside-out because American diners kept peeling the seaweed off, and Japan imported it back.

dishes.label: Callaloo
dishes.origin: Its name may come from an Angolan word for okra; the leafy stew blends West African and Taino roots and is a national dish of two islands.

dishes.label: Calzone
dishes.origin: The name means 'trouser leg' or 'sock', for the way the folded pizza looks; it is baked, not fried, and the Apulian fried cousin is the panzerotto.

dishes.label: Caponata
dishes.origin: A sweet-and-sour Sicilian eggplant stew tied to the island's Jewish community; one grand old version came with lobster and swordfish.

dishes.label: Carbonade flamande
dishes.origin: Belgium's beer-braised beef is thickened with bread, and in East and West Flanders cooks often slip in prunes while it stews.

dishes.label: Carbonara
dishes.origin: Nobody printed the name before the Second World War; it likely came from Allied soldiers' bacon and eggs meeting Roman spaghetti.

dishes.label: Carpaccio
dishes.origin: Harry's Bar in Venice invented it in 1950 for a countess told to eat raw meat, naming it for a painter famed for red and white tones.

dishes.label: Cassoulet
dishes.origin: Legend says it was invented in 1355 in besieged Castelnaudary; a brotherhood there still guards the recipe and throws a festival.

dishes.label: Cendol
dishes.origin: Green pandan jelly strands are pressed through a sieve into cold water; Thailand's version, lot chong, means 'gone through a hole'.

dishes.label: Ćevapi
dishes.origin: Bosnia and Serbia both call it national; Sarajevo's beef version won EU-style geographic protection in 2024, and Banja Luka serves four joined in a row.

dishes.label: Ceviche
dishes.origin: Peru gave ceviche its own holiday, and its ancient coastal people may have soured fish with banana passionfruit juice long before limes arrived.

dishes.label: Chaat
dishes.origin: Mughal court doctors are said to have urged Delhi to eat spicy fried snacks with yogurt to balance the Yamuna river's alkaline water.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Papri Chaat (Crispy Indian Snack with Potato)

dishes.label: Challah
dishes.origin: Its braid may echo the hair of the Sabbath bride, and two loaves sit on the table to recall the double portion of manna in the desert.

dishes.label: Chalupa
dishes.origin: Named for the boat it resembles; in Cholula the little fried masa boats carry only salsa, cheese and lettuce, nothing like the fast-food version.

dishes.label: Chana masala
dishes.origin: This chickpea curry is the 'chole' half of chole bhature, soaked overnight and cooked in a tangy tomato gravy across North India and Pakistan.

dishes.label: Chankonabe
dishes.origin: The sumo wrestlers' bulking-up hotpot; at tournaments it is made only with chicken, so a wrestler stays on two legs, never on all fours.

dishes.label: Chapli kebab
dishes.origin: Named for the Pashto word for flat, or maybe for a sandal sole, this Peshawar patty is traditionally fried in animal fat over wood fires.

dishes.label: Char siu
dishes.origin: Its name means fork-roasted, and the red colour once came from fermented bean curd and red yeast rice, not the food colouring used today.

dishes.label: Chazuke
dishes.origin: Japan's tea-poured-over-rice snack began as a quick way for merchants' apprentices to finish cold leftover rice; in Kyoto it is called bubuzuke.

dishes.label: Chess pie
dishes.origin: A Southern desperation pie made from pantry basics; nobody knows if its name came from cheese, a pie chest or a mumbled it's just pie.

dishes.label: Chicago-Style Hot Dog
dishes.origin: Called 'dragged through the garden' for its pile of toppings; ketchup is the one thing many Chicago vendors refuse to put on it.

dishes.label: Chicken à la King
dishes.place: Philadelphia or New York, United States
dishes.origin: Its birthplace is argued over, but it began as a posh 1890s hotel dish and ended as a 1950s buffet staple, later called retro comfort food.

dishes.label: Chicken fried steak
dishes.origin: German and Austrian settlers in Texas turned schnitzel into this; Lamesa, Texas, still holds a yearly party claiming it was born there.

dishes.label: Chicken paprikash
dishes.origin: Its first known recipe appeared in an 1830 Hungarian cookbook; the sour cream sets it apart from paprika-stew cousins like goulash and pörkölt.

dishes.label: Chicken tikka
dishes.origin: Said to date from the Mughal emperor Babur's reign; its name is Persian for 'pieces'. Britain later turned it into chicken tikka masala.

dishes.label: Chicken tikka masala
dishes.origin: Britain's Foreign Secretary once called it a true national dish, yet Glasgow and the Punjab still argue over who invented it.

dishes.label: Chilaquiles
dishes.origin: Made to rescue leftover tortillas, and in Guadalajara the pot simmers until it turns thick like polenta.

dishes.label: Chile relleno
dishes.origin: The name just means stuffed chile, and an 1858 description already had a green pepper filled with minced meat and coated in egg.

dishes.label: Chiles en nogada
dishes.origin: Green pepper, white sauce and red pomegranate seeds mirror Mexico's flag; Puebla's nuns are said to have first made it for Emperor Iturbide in 1821.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Chiles en Nogada (Stuffed Chile Peppers with Almonds)

dishes.label: Chili con carne
dishes.origin: Texas made it the state dish in 1977, and fans still feud over whether beans or tomatoes belong anywhere near it.

dishes.label: Chimichanga
dishes.origin: Legend says Tucson's Monica Flin dropped a burrito in the fryer around 1950, and a rival in Phoenix claims he did it first in 1946.

dishes.label: Chimney cake
dishes.origin: Named for a stovepipe, it is wound on a spit and rolled in sugar; the caramel crust only caught on in the 1800s.

dishes.label: Cholent
dishes.place: Jewish communities of France and Germany
dishes.origin: A Sabbath stew first named in 1180; families once took pots to the baker's always-hot oven on Friday and collected the cooked stew on Saturday morning.

dishes.label: Chop suey
dishes.origin: Nobody agrees who invented it, and its name once meant offal in Cantonese; St. Louis still has chop suey joints.

dishes.label: Chow mein
dishes.origin: Chinese migrants carried it to California during the gold rush; in the 1940s a canned version swapped costly water chestnuts for celery.

dishes.label: Christmas pudding
dishes.origin: Hidden silver coins were once stirred in for luck; the 1927 royal recipe used rum from Jamaica, currants from Australia and apples from Canada.

dishes.label: Çiğ köfte
dishes.origin: Urfa's spicy raw-meat meze was banned in meat form in 2008; it is now sold meatless, rolled in lettuce with lemon.

dishes.label: Cincinnati chili
dishes.origin: Greek immigrant brothers started it in 1922 as a hot dog topping; it holds no chocolate despite the myth, and you order it in ways.

dishes.label: Cioppino
dishes.origin: Fishermen back from Meiggs Wharf with empty nets passed a pot around, and everyone chipped something in.

dishes.label: Clafoutis
dishes.origin: Limousin cooks traditionally leave the cherry stones in, which lends a faint almond flavour from the kernels.

dishes.label: Clam chowder
dishes.origin: Boston's creamy white and Manhattan's red tomato versions are rivals, and Rhode Island makes a clear one with neither milk nor tomato.

dishes.label: Cobb salad
dishes.origin: Legend says restaurateur Robert Cobb raided the Brown Derby kitchen near midnight in 1937 and chopped the leftovers together.

dishes.label: Cochinita pibil
dishes.origin: Yucatec Maya cooks buried it in a pit oven called a píib; the name means 'baby pig', and bitter Seville oranges are the signature.

dishes.label: Coq au vin
dishes.origin: Legends tie it to Julius Caesar's Gaul, but the first recorded recipe is a century old; Julia Child's TV cooking made it a signature American dish.

dishes.label: Cornish pasty
dishes.origin: Miners reputedly rewarmed theirs on a shovel over a candle; since 2011 only pasties made in Cornwall may carry the name under EU protection.

dishes.label: Coronation chicken
dishes.origin: Two Cordon Bleu School cooks made it for the 1953 coronation banquet of Queen Elizabeth II; the first version used apricot puree, not raisins.

dishes.label: Couscous
dishes.origin: Hand-rolled semolina is steamed over a stew in a couscoussier; UNESCO listed the skill in 2020 for four North African countries together.

dishes.label: Coxinha
dishes.origin: Its name means 'little thigh'; the tale says a cook shaped chicken into drumsticks for a royal child who ate nothing else.

dishes.label: Crab cake
dishes.origin: Maryland claims it, and Baltimore crab cakes were on a 1939 World's Fair cookbook menu; true Marylanders use almost no filler.

dishes.label: Cranachan
dishes.origin: Once a harvest-time treat for August raspberries; it grew out of crowdie cheese and toasted oatmeal, and diners assemble their own.

dishes.label: Crème brûlée
dishes.origin: A 1691 French cookbook gives the first known recipe, yet Trinity College, Cambridge, once branded its crest into the sugar crust.

dishes.label: Croque monsieur
dishes.origin: A Paris cafe fixture whose name means crunch-mister; a fried egg on top turns it into a croque madame, and an 1891 magazine already mentions it.

dishes.label: Croquette
dishes.origin: The first printed recipe appeared in 1691 from the chef of Louis XIV, who bound truffles, sweetbreads and cream into a crunchy roll.

dishes.label: Cullen skink
dishes.origin: Named for a fishing town in Moray where fishermen made use of plentiful haddock; skink is a Scots word for a shin of beef.

dishes.label: Daifuku
dishes.origin: Its name means great luck, a pun on the old belly-shaped rice cake it began as; the strawberry version only appeared in the 1980s.

dishes.label: Dal makhani
dishes.origin: Moti Mahal's founders in Delhi made it in the early 1950s as a vegetarian partner for their butter chicken; its name means buttery lentils.

dishes.label: Dango
dishes.origin: The proverb 'hana yori dango' says a dumpling beats flowers; the pink, white and green skewer is the one eaten under cherry blossoms.

dishes.label: Danish pastry
dishes.origin: Denmark calls it Viennese bread: a bakers' strike in 1850 brought Austrian bakers in, and their lamination know-how stayed.

dishes.label: Dhokla
dishes.origin: A pulse-cake ancestor shows up in a Jain text from 1066, and Ahmedabad has been said to eat 10,000 kilos of dhokla a day.

dishes.label: Dirty rice
dishes.origin: It gets its dirty look from finely chopped chicken livers and gizzards; Louisiana cooks once made it from the cuts nobody else wanted.

dishes.label: Dolma
dishes.origin: Ottoman palace cooks perfected stuffing vegetables; Armenians, Greeks and Turks all claim it, and Sweden's cabbage rolls came home with Charles XII.

dishes.label: Doner kebab
dishes.origin: Turkish cooks turned the roasting spit upright in the 1800s; Berlin's guest workers later stuffed it into bread, creating the city's signature snack.

dishes.label: Dosa
dishes.origin: Its batter is fermented, and in 2014 twenty-nine chefs in Hyderabad set a record by making a giant one.

dishes.label: Doubles
dishes.origin: Street-food king of Trinidad: in 1936 a vendor's customers kept asking for a second bara, and the name 'doubles' stuck.

dishes.label: Douhua
dishes.origin: Once called tofu brains for its softness, it is sweet in the south, salty in the north and fiery in Sichuan, and in the Philippines it becomes taho.

dishes.label: Drunken noodles
dishes.origin: Its name means drunkard, yet there is no alcohol in it; one tale says a wife loaded it with chilies to teach her husband a lesson.

dishes.label: Egg foo young
dishes.origin: Its name means 'hibiscus egg'. In St. Louis it is a sandwich: a foo young patty with mayo and pickle between white bread.

dishes.label: Eggs Benedict
dishes.origin: Three men claim to have invented it, from a hungover Wall Street broker at the Waldorf in 1894 to Delmonico's, which says 1860.

dishes.label: Egusi soup
dishes.origin: The Yoruba name means 'grind open', after the way the pale melon seeds are pounded to thicken the pot.

dishes.label: Ekmek kadayıfı
dishes.origin: A frugal use of stale bread from Afyonkarahisar, served at Ramadan iftar and crowned with clotted cream.

dishes.label: Enchilada
dishes.origin: The original street version was just a tortilla dipped in chili sauce; the name literally means 'seasoned with chili'.

dishes.label: Ensaimada
dishes.origin: Mallorca's coiled pastry takes its name from saim, the pork lard in the dough; in the Philippines the same pastry is topped with cheese.

dishes.label: Fajita
dishes.origin: Texas ranch hands were handed scrap skirt steak in the 1930s; the word fajita, little belt, did not appear in print until 1971.

dishes.label: Falafel
dishes.origin: Likely born in Egypt; rationing in 1949 made this cheap bean fritter a hit in Israel, and now Israelis and Palestinians both claim it.

dishes.label: Falooda
dishes.origin: It began as Persian faloodeh, then Mughal courts in India added milk and rose syrup. Today it is a cold dessert drink from Karachi to Colombo to Yangon.

dishes.label: Farofa
dishes.origin: Toasted cassava flour is sprinkled on Brazilian feijoada and churrasco at the table, the way other cultures reach for rice.

dishes.label: Fattoush
dishes.origin: Its name comes from the Arabic for crush, and a 10th-century Baghdad cookbook has a dish of crumbled bread and cucumber that looks like its ancestor.

dishes.label: Feijoada
dishes.origin: Brazil's national stew is first documented in Recife in 1827, and in Rio it is a traditional Friday lunch.

dishes.label: Fesenjān
dishes.origin: A rich Persian walnut-and-pomegranate stew, a Yalda Night favourite; Iranians mock a show-off as acting like they have had partridge and fesenjān.

dishes.label: Filipino spaghetti
dishes.origin: American-era spaghetti Bolognese was sweetened with banana ketchup after wartime tomato shortages; now it is the birthday-party staple.

dishes.label: Fondue
dishes.origin: A 1930s Swiss Cheese Union campaign made it the national dish; lose your bread in the pot and you owe a round of drinks.

dishes.label: Francesinha
dishes.origin: Created in Porto in 1953 by a man home from France and Belgium who wanted a Portuguese croque monsieur, drowned in a beer-and-tomato sauce.

dishes.label: French onion soup
dishes.origin: The cheese-crusted version was born around Paris's Les Halles market, though earlier versions of onion soup go back to Roman times and a 1393 Parisian recipe.

dishes.label: French tacos
dishes.origin: Despite the name it is nothing like a Mexican taco; the filled, grilled tortilla was born around Lyon and is nicknamed the mattress.

dishes.label: Ful medames
dishes.origin: Cairo's night-simmering pots were heated by bathhouse embers, and the beans were sold wholesale for the city's breakfast.

dishes.label: Full English Breakfast
dishes.origin: Cooked breakfasts burst onto the scene in Victorian Britain; some say the 'Full Monty' honours General Montgomery, who ate one daily in Africa.

dishes.label: Funeral potatoes
dishes.place: Utah and the Intermountain West, United States
dishes.origin: This cheesy casserole is a staple of Utah funerals and potlucks, and it even got its own souvenir pin at the 2002 Winter Olympics.

dishes.label: Gado-gado
dishes.origin: Its name roughly means eaten without rice, so lontong rice cake stands in; Indonesia named it one of five national dishes in 2018.

dishes.label: Gajar ka halwa
dishes.origin: This carrot sweet turns up at Diwali, Holi and Eid, and it is a winter treat served hot.

dishes.label: Galaktoboureko
dishes.origin: Unlike a mille-feuille, the custard bakes inside the filo; some say it began in Smyrna, and Turkey's Black Sea coast has its own peppery version.

dishes.label: Galbi
dishes.origin: Korean barbecue's rib classic; the thin cross-cut 'LA galbi' is said to have been born in Los Angeles' Koreatown, then sailed back to Seoul.

dishes.label: Gallo pinto
dishes.origin: Costa Rica and Nicaragua each cooked huge batches to claim it, and the rivalry is sometimes called the Gallo Pinto War.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Gallo Pinto (Costa Rican Rice and Beans)

dishes.label: Gazpacho
dishes.origin: Spanish farmhands pounded bread, oil and garlic into a cold soup long before tomatoes arrived from the Americas turned it red.

dishes.label: Gefilte fish
dishes.origin: It began as stuffed pike in a 14th-century German cookbook, and a sweet-versus-peppery split once divided Polish Jews along the so-called Gefilte Fish Line.

dishes.label: German chocolate cake
dishes.origin: It is not German at all: it was named for Samuel German, the Boston baker whose sweet baking chocolate it used, and was born in a 1950s Dallas newspaper.

dishes.label: Ghormeh sabzi
dishes.origin: Called Iran's national dish, this herb stew is at least 2,500 years old and was the first Iranian dish eaten in space.

dishes.label: Gimbap
dishes.origin: Korea rolls it with sesame oil and salt where Japan uses vinegar; frozen packs sold out at Trader Joe's in 2023.

dishes.label: Gingerbread
dishes.origin: Legend says an Armenian monk, Gregory of Nicopolis, taught French bakers gingerbread near Pithiviers around 992.

dishes.label: Giouvetsi
dishes.origin: Named for the Turkish clay pot it bakes in; Paula Wolfert called it one of the most famous Greek island lamb dishes.

dishes.label: Gnocchi
dishes.origin: Its name may come from the Italian for a knot in wood or a knuckle, yet the potato version is barely 150 years old, since the Romans used flour.

dishes.label: Gobi Manchurian
dishes.origin: Not from Manchuria at all: a cook at Mumbai's Cricket Club of India reportedly improvised it in 1975 with soy sauce instead of garam masala.

dishes.label: Gordita
dishes.origin: The name means 'chubby'. Masa pockets are traditionally stuffed with chicharrón, and Durango makes them from wheat flour.

dishes.label: Goulash
dishes.origin: Hungarian cattle herders cooked it in kettles over open fires; the name comes from 'gulyas', a cattleman, and paprika only joined later.

dishes.label: Gözleme
dishes.origin: Its name comes from an old word for cooking on embers, and Turkish cooks fill the thin dough with everything from spinach to pastirma.

dishes.label: Green curry
dishes.origin: Its Thai name means sweet green, and the sweet refers to the colour, not the taste; the curry took shape around the reign of Rama VI or VII.

dishes.label: Guacamole
dishes.origin: Its name is Nahuatl for avocado sauce; an English pirate wrote down a version in 1697, with sugar in it.

dishes.label: Gulab jamun
dishes.origin: A Mughal-era sweet whose name nods to rosewater syrup (gulab); in Bengal the dark fried version is Pantua, and Nepal calls it Lal Mohan.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Gulab Jamun (Fried Milk Balls in Syrup)

dishes.label: Gumbo
dishes.origin: Its name likely comes from a West African word for okra, and a 1970s Senate dining room menu helped make this Louisiana stew a national star.

dishes.label: Gyros
dishes.origin: Its name means 'turn', copying Turkish döner; Greek refugees from Asia Minor brought the spit to Greece, and Chicago made it a US craze by 1970.

dishes.label: Gyudon
dishes.origin: Japan's fast-food beef bowl grew from Tokyo's beef hotpots; after the 1923 earthquake 'the whole nation ate gyudon'. Yoshinoya opened in 1899.

dishes.label: Haggis
dishes.origin: Robert Burns made it Scotland's national dish with a poem in 1786, and a poll found a third of American visitors thought it was a small animal.

dishes.label: Hainanese chicken rice
dishes.origin: Born of frugality, it used old hens poached for broth; Singapore and Malaysia still squabble over who invented it.

dishes.label: Haleem
dishes.origin: Hyderabadi haleem was the first Indian meat product to win a GI tag; it is stirred for hours in huge Ramadan cauldrons.

dishes.label: Halo-Halo
dishes.origin: Grew out of a Japanese shaved-ice dessert sold near Manila's ice plant in the 1920s; its name just means 'mix-mix'.

dishes.label: Halva
dishes.origin: Its name means sweet in Arabic; in the 7th century it was a paste of dates kneaded with milk, and today it spans from sesame bricks to carrot pudding.

dishes.label: Head cheese
dishes.origin: It contains no dairy at all; the English name is a calque of the Dutch hoofdkaas, and meat jellies like it have fed peasants since the Middle Ages.

dishes.label: Hoppin' John
dishes.origin: A Gullah one-pot eaten on New Year's Day for luck; the peas stand for coins and the greens on the side for paper money.

dishes.label: Horseshoe sandwich
dishes.origin: Springfield, Illinois invented this open-faced pile, first with ham; the name comes from a bone-in ham slice or a horseshoe of potatoes.

dishes.label: Hot and sour soup
dishes.origin: Descended from Henan's peppery hulatang; the American Chinese takeout version is thicker thanks to cornstarch, and the Sichuan claim is mostly myth.

dishes.label: Hot cross bun
dishes.origin: A 1592 London decree banned spiced buns except at funerals, Good Friday and Christmas; folklore says a Good Friday bun never goes moldy.

dishes.label: Hot Pot
dishes.origin: Said to trace to bronze pots of the Zhou nobles; Emperor Qianlong ate it at nearly every meal, and a Qing coronation fed 1,550 pots at once.

dishes.label: Huevos rancheros
dishes.origin: Early recipes from the 1800s had no tortillas at all, just eggs cooked in red or green chile sauce; the tortilla came later.

dishes.label: Hummus
dishes.origin: Lebanon, Israel and Syria all claim it; the oldest written recipes are 13th-century Syrian and 14th-century Cairo, and garlic was a late arrival.

dishes.label: Hushpuppy
dishes.origin: One tale says Southern fishermen tossed the fried cornmeal balls to their barking dogs to hush them; Puerto Rico's cousin is the sorullo.

dishes.label: Idli
dishes.origin: Idli's steamed rice-and-lentil batter may have been fermented in Indonesia first, a theory food historians still argue over.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Idli (Steamed Rice and Black Gram Bread)

dishes.label: Israeli salad
dishes.origin: Kibbutz cooks prized the finest, most perfect dice of tomato and cucumber; the dish grew from Ottoman-era Palestine salads.

dishes.label: Italian wedding soup
dishes.origin: Its name is a mistranslation: minestra maritata means 'married soup', for the marriage of meat and greens, and it has nothing to do with weddings.

dishes.label: Jägerschnitzel
dishes.origin: 'Hunter's schnitzel': in East Germany the school-canteen version was not meat at all but a fried slice of Jagdwurst sausage with ketchup.

dishes.label: Jalebi
dishes.place: Persia and the Arab world, now South Asia
dishes.origin: A tenth-century Arabic cookbook already had a fritter in syrup; it traveled to India, where batter is piped into orange spirals.

dishes.label: Jalfrezi
dishes.origin: Born in Bengal under the Raj as a way to fry up cold leftover meat; it later became the most ordered dish in British curry houses in 2011.

dishes.label: Jamaican patty
dishes.origin: A 1985 Canadian row over the name 'beef patty' ended when vendors agreed to call it a Jamaican patty. It mixes Cornish pasty and Spanish turnover ideas.

dishes.label: Jambalaya
dishes.origin: Nobody agrees if its name means a mix-up in Provencal or ham with rice; New Orleans cooks it red with tomato, Cajun country brown.

dishes.label: Japanese curry
dishes.origin: The British Navy's curry came to Japan in the 1800s; the Imperial Navy thickened it with flour, and today it outsells sushi and tempura at the table.

dishes.label: Japchae
dishes.origin: A 1600s king loved it so much he promoted its maker; the original had no noodles, which only arrived once Chinese sweet potato starch noodles came along.

dishes.label: Jian dui
dishes.origin: A Tang dynasty court snack that traveled south with migrants; it puffs into a hollow ball when fried and shows up as onde-onde, buchi and goma dango.

dishes.label: Jianbing
dishes.origin: Legend says Zhuge Liang's soldiers lost their woks and cooked batter on their shields; Tianjin's version tops it with a fried dough stick.

dishes.label: Jiaozi
dishes.origin: Said to be named for 'tender ears', and eaten at midnight on New Year's Eve because they resemble old gold ingots.

dishes.label: Jjamppong
dishes.origin: A Korean-Chinese noodle soup whose name came from Japanese chanpon; its fiery red broth only took off in the 1960s.

dishes.label: Johnny Marzetti
dishes.origin: Ohio's casserole is tied to a Columbus Italian restaurant by legend, but the restaurant's own company has found no record of it.

dishes.label: Jollof rice
dishes.origin: Nigeria and Ghana feud over who cooks the best one in the so-called Jollof Wars; Jamie Oliver's 2014 version sparked #jollofgate.

dishes.label: Kabsa
dishes.origin: Its name means to press, because everything cooks squeezed into one pot; Saudi Arabia launched a drive in 2021 to promote it as national heritage.

dishes.label: Kaiserschmarrn
dishes.origin: The 'Emperor's Mess' is said to be named for Franz Joseph I, who loved the fluffy torn-up pancake; one tale has his dieting wife refusing it.

dishes.label: Kaldereta
dishes.origin: The name comes from the Spanish caldera, the pot of a Spanish fish and goat stew, remade in the Philippines with local ingredients and liver paste.

dishes.label: Karaage
dishes.origin: Japan's marinated, starch-dusted fried chicken. Every year over 60 shops compete at the Karaage Festival in Nakatsu, and Lawson sells it at the till.

dishes.label: Karelian pasty
dishes.origin: Finland's rye-crusted rice pies carry EU protected status, and are only the real thing with egg butter spread over them hot.

dishes.label: Katsudon
dishes.origin: Students eat it before big exams because katsu also means to win, and Japanese cop films love a katsudon confession scene.

dishes.label: Kedgeree
dishes.origin: Descended from India's rice-and-lentil khichri, Britons brought it home as a Victorian breakfast; recipes appear in Scotland as early as 1790.

dishes.label: Khachapuri
dishes.origin: Georgians love it so much that an economics school tracks the price of making one as a local inflation index.

dishes.label: Khao soi
dishes.origin: Chin Haw Muslim caravan traders from Yunnan likely brought it to the north; its Burmese cousin is ohn no khao swe, and the Lao version has no coconut at all.

dishes.label: Kheer
dishes.origin: Served to pilgrims at Kerala's Ambalapuzha temple, thanks to a legend of Krishna and a chessboard of rice grains.

dishes.label: Khichdi
dishes.origin: A rice-and-lentil comfort dish that Ibn Battuta described in 1350; babies often get it as a first solid food, and it inspired kedgeree.

dishes.label: Kibbeh
dishes.origin: Lebanon and Syria both claim it; Aleppo alone boasts dozens of kinds, and Brazil's Arab immigrants even made it with rice flour.

dishes.label: Kimchi
dishes.origin: Chili peppers only reached Korea in the early 1600s, so the fiery red kimchi we know is younger than many people think.

dishes.label: Kimchi jjigae
dishes.origin: Cooks prize old, sour kimchi for it, and the army-base version is stuffed with Spam and hot dogs from Korean War surplus.

dishes.label: King cake
dishes.place: Epiphany tradition across Europe and Louisiana
dishes.origin: Whoever finds the hidden bean or baby figurine is king for the day, or pays for next year's cake. New Orleans bakers made it a Mardi Gras icon.

dishes.label: Knafeh
dishes.origin: Nablus is crowned the knafeh capital, yet the first cheese-filled recipe in print only dates from an 1885 Beirut cookbook.

dishes.label: Knish
dishes.place: Eastern Europe and New York City
dishes.origin: Ukrainians baked it for Christmas Eve; Jewish immigrants made it a New York street-cart staple in the 1900s.

dishes.label: Kokoretsi
dishes.origin: Byzantine cooks were already wrapping offal in braided lamb intestine; Greeks roast it for Easter, Turks sell it in a bun from street kiosks.

dishes.label: Kolache
dishes.origin: Czech wedding treats whose name means wheel; Texas and Minnesota towns both claim to be the kolache capital.

dishes.label: Korma
dishes.origin: A braise from the Mughal court kitchens whose name means braising, not curry; in Indonesia the korma has no dates, even though kurma means date.

dishes.label: Korokke
dishes.origin: Japan borrowed the French croquette in 1887; in the 2000s a forum post made eating it before a typhoon a social-media tradition.

dishes.label: Koshari
dishes.origin: Egypt's national street dish piles rice, pasta and lentils in one bowl; UNESCO added it to its cultural heritage list in 2025.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Koshary (Egyptian Pasta Salad with Rice and Lentils)

dishes.label: Kugel
dishes.origin: The name means 'ball' in old German; early kugels were savory bread puddings before noodles, raisins and cottage cheese arrived.

dishes.label: Kung Pao chicken
dishes.origin: Named for Ding Baozhen, a Qing governor of Sichuan titled Gongbao; the 'ding' in the dish's name puns on his surname and on its diced cubes.

dishes.label: Laddu
dishes.origin: Described as perhaps India's oldest, most universal sweet; a 2016 laddu in Andhra Pradesh weighed 29,465 kilograms.

dishes.label: Lahmacun
dishes.origin: A 13th-century Aleppo cookbook gives the earliest known recipe for thin dough with minced meat, baked in a brick oven. Its name means 'meat with dough'.

dishes.label: Laksa
dishes.origin: Born when Chinese traders married local women in the Straits ports; the word may come from a Persian term for 'slippery' noodles.

dishes.label: Lamington
dishes.origin: Named for a Queensland governor, Lord Lamington, it may have been invented by his French chef from leftover sponge, and has its own National Day on 21 July.

dishes.label: Lángos
dishes.origin: Its name means flamed: Hungarian bakers cooked it in the morning while the big oven was still heating for the weekly bread.

dishes.label: Larb
dishes.origin: Laos's national dish is a lucky one: its name sounds like the word for good fortune, so families eat it on New Year's first day.

dishes.label: Lasagna
dishes.origin: The oldest written mention is a 1282 Bolognese ballad; in Bologna the sheets are traditionally green, coloured with spinach or nettles.

dishes.label: Latke
dishes.origin: Before potatoes reached Eastern Europe, Hanukkah latkes were made of cheese, and they are fried to recall the temple oil.

dishes.label: Laziji
dishes.origin: Truck drivers and travellers made this chicken famous in Geleshan; the diner hunts for the nuggets of chicken buried in a mountain of chilies.

dishes.label: Leberkäse
dishes.origin: Despite the name ('liver cheese'), there is usually neither liver nor cheese; Bavarians eat it in a roll with sweet mustard.

dishes.label: Lebkuchen
dishes.origin: Franconian monks baked these honey cookies by the 1200s; true Nuremberg Elisenlebkuchen need at least 25 percent nuts and hardly any flour.

dishes.label: Lecsó
dishes.origin: Hungary's peppers-and-tomato stew is best cooked over an open fire in a cauldron, and the country holds festivals for it.

dishes.label: Linzertorte
dishes.origin: Its recipe dates to 1653, which makes it a contender for the oldest cake named after a place.

dishes.label: Litti Chokha
dishes.origin: Bihar's smoky street food: roasted dough balls with mashed vegetables, said to be eaten by Lord Ram himself and sent to a Manila street-food event.

dishes.label: Lo mein
dishes.origin: Its Cantonese name means stirred noodles; unlike chow mein, the Cantonese original is boiled and tossed, never fried crisp.

dishes.label: Lobster Thermidor
dishes.origin: Named after an 1891 Paris play called Thermidor; it later turned up in Citizen Kane as a symbol of fancy dining.

dishes.label: Loukoumades
dishes.origin: Honey-soaked fried dough balls go back to ancient Greece and 13th-century Baghdad, where they were called the judge's morsels.

dishes.label: Lumpia
dishes.origin: Fujianese settlers brought the soft 'wet cake' roll to Java; each Indonesian city fills it differently, Semarang with bamboo shoots.

dishes.label: Luosifen
dishes.origin: Liuzhou's snail noodle soup rarely holds snail meat; its famous stink comes from fermented bamboo shoots, and instant packs sell by the million.

dishes.label: Macaron
dishes.origin: Two Carmelite nuns sold them in 1790s Nancy to pay for lodgings during the Revolution; the filled sandwich version only arrived in the 20th century.

dishes.label: Madras curry
dishes.origin: Madras curry was invented by Anglo-Indian cooks, and the name is not used in India itself.

dishes.label: Malva pudding
dishes.origin: A Cape sponge soaked in hot cream sauce; one chef's nickname for it, telefoenpoeding, comes from farm wives reading the recipe down the phone.

dishes.label: Manakish
dishes.origin: Levantine women once baked dough in the village oven each morning; Lebanon won a UNESCO listing for the tradition in 2023.

dishes.label: Manjū
dishes.origin: Monks who brought the bun from China swapped its meat filling for sweet beans, since Zen monks could not eat meat.

dishes.label: Mansaf
dishes.origin: Jordan's national dish, eaten standing, right hand only. Rival tribes sealed truces over a shared platter, and UNESCO listed it in 2022.

dishes.label: Manti
dishes.origin: Said to be carried across the Silk Road by horsemen with frozen dumplings; Turks serve tiny ones with garlic yogurt and melted butter.

dishes.label: Mapo doufu
dishes.origin: Named for the pockmarked grandmother who ran a Chengdu restaurant in the 1800s; Japan fell for it when Iron Chef's Chen Kenichi made it famous on TV.

dishes.label: Masala dosa
dishes.origin: A Udupi restaurateur in 1930s Madras made it famous, though potatoes only reached India with the Portuguese, so the royal-kitchen legend is off.

dishes.label: Massaman curry
dishes.origin: Its name is a twist on the Persian word for Muslim; the dish is tied to a Persian merchant at Ayutthaya's court, and CNN once ranked it the world's best food.

dishes.label: Maultaschen
dishes.origin: Swabians joke the meat is hidden under the pasta so God can't see it on Good Friday, hence the nickname small God-cheaters.

dishes.label: Meatloaf
dishes.origin: American meatloaf descends from German-American scrapple, and Depression-era cooks stretched the meat with crackers and bread.

dishes.label: Menemen
dishes.origin: Turkey's tomato-and-egg breakfast pan is named for the town of Menemen, and a 2018 Twitter poll on whether to add onions split the nation.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Menemen (Eggs with Onion, Green Pepper, and Tomato)

dishes.label: Menudo
dishes.origin: A Mexican tripe soup with Spanish roots, long served as a weekend hangover cure; Santa Maria, California holds an annual Menudo Festival.

dishes.label: Mie goreng
dishes.origin: Chinese immigrants brought chow mein to Indonesia; cooks added sweet soy sauce and fried shallots, and swapped pork for chicken or shrimp.

dishes.label: Migas
dishes.origin: Shepherds on the move made these from stale bread over small braziers. Mexico and Texas use the same name for eggs scrambled with crisp tortilla.

dishes.label: Milanesa
dishes.origin: Argentines eat milanesas about three times a week; the napolitana, with tomato sauce, ham and cheese, may have hidden a burnt cutlet.

dishes.label: Mille-Feuille
dishes.origin: The name means 'thousand sheets'; 18th-century versions were stacked with jam, and Careme later refined the cream-filled form we know.

dishes.label: Mince pie
dishes.origin: Old versions held minced mutton or tongue with fruit; today's has no meat, and some Britons say you must never cut one or you cut your luck.

dishes.label: Mincemeat
dishes.origin: Early English mincemeat really was minced mutton or beef with fruit; most jars today contain no meat at all.

dishes.label: Minestrone
dishes.origin: A cucina povera classic with no fixed recipe; its Roman ancestors were vegetable and farro porridges, and tomatoes only joined after Columbus.

dishes.label: Misal pav
dishes.origin: Maharashtra's spicy sprouted-bean breakfast; Kolhapur's fiery version is legendary, and a Mumbai plate won a London award in 2015.

dishes.label: Miso soup
dishes.origin: More than 80 percent of Japan's miso ends up in this soup; add pork and it becomes tonjiru, and it sits beside white rice at a traditional breakfast.

dishes.label: Mock turtle soup
dishes.origin: Invented in the 1700s to imitate pricey green turtle soup, it never had turtle in it; Cincinnati still loves it.

dishes.label: Modak
dishes.origin: Offered by the 21 or 101 at Ganesh Chaturthi because Ganesha loves them; old texts say they looked like hailstones.

dishes.label: Mofongo
dishes.origin: Its name likely comes from a Kikongo word for 'a great amount of anything', and a 1980 tourist booklet called it a Puerto Rican matzoh ball.

dishes.label: Molokhia
dishes.origin: A slimy-green jute-leaf stew from ancient Egypt; the Fatimid ruler al-Hakim banned it around 1005, thinking it an aphrodisiac.

dishes.label: Momo
dishes.origin: Nepal and Tibet each claim these steamed dumplings; one legend says a Nepali princess carried them over the Himalaya in the 7th century.

dishes.label: Mont Blanc
dishes.origin: A Paris pastry named for the Alpine peak: chestnut vermicelli piled up and capped with cream like snow. Escoffier said to heap the cream roughly.

dishes.label: Monte Cristo
dishes.origin: A 1923 trade magazine already named it, and Disneyland's Blue Bayou restaurant helped make it famous; it is a fried American cousin of the croque monsieur.

dishes.label: Moo shu pork
dishes.origin: Named for sweet osmanthus blossoms, which the scrambled egg was said to resemble; the Shandong original had bamboo shoots.

dishes.label: Mooncake
dishes.origin: Eaten at the Mid-Autumn Festival, a mooncake's salted egg yolk stands for the full moon, and some versions carry four yolks for the moon's phases.

dishes.label: Moqueca
dishes.origin: Bahia's version needs dendê palm oil and coconut milk from Africa; Espírito Santo cooks use annatto and insist on a black clay pot.

dishes.label: Moules-frites
dishes.origin: Lille's braderie gets through about 500 tons of mussels in one weekend, with the empty shells piled up outside the restaurants.

dishes.label: Moussaka
dishes.origin: The famous Greek version with its creamy white top is barely a century old, invented in the 1920s by a French-trained chef, Nikolaos Tselementes.

dishes.label: Muesli
dishes.origin: Swiss doctor Bircher-Benner served it to hospital patients around 1900, inspired by a dish from an Alpine hike; it began as an appetiser.

dishes.label: Muffuletta
dishes.origin: Said to have been invented in 1906 at New Orleans' Central Grocery by a Sicilian immigrant; its olive salad is the signature.

dishes.label: Muhammara
dishes.origin: The name means something that has turned red; Aleppo's red pepper and walnut dip is now a protected specialty of Gaziantep, Turkey.

dishes.label: Mulligatawny
dishes.origin: The name means pepper-water in Tamil; British cooks in India added chicken and mutton, and by 1827 it was a London fashion.

dishes.label: Murtabak
dishes.origin: Its Arabic name means 'folded'. Tamil Muslim traders likely carried it from Yemen to Southeast Asia, where mamak stalls serve it with curry.

dishes.label: Naengmyeon
dishes.origin: A northern Korean winter treat that became a summer favorite; Kim Jong Un once brought Pyongyang noodles to a summit as a gift.

dishes.label: Nanaimo bar
dishes.origin: This no-bake Canadian treat once appeared as the main dessert at a 2016 White House state dinner and later on a Canada Post stamp.

dishes.label: Nasi goreng
dishes.origin: Indonesia's national dish began as thrifty Chinese-style leftover rice, then gained sweet soy sauce, shrimp paste and a fried egg on top.

dishes.label: Nasi lemak
dishes.origin: Malaysia's national breakfast, wrapped in banana leaf; one legend says a girl spilled coconut milk into her rice and said just rice, Mom.

dishes.label: Neapolitan ragù
dishes.origin: Naples calls it the queen of sauces; it simmers for hours on Sunday and was once nicknamed for the doorkeeper, the only one with time to watch it.

dishes.label: Oden
dishes.origin: Some shops simmer the same oden broth as a master stock for years. In Nagoya it still means a miso stew, and 7-Eleven sells it from the counter.

dishes.label: Okonomiyaki
dishes.origin: Its name means 'as you like it'; after 1945 Hiroshima cooks made it from whatever they could get, and the city now has over 2,000 okonomiyaki shops.

dishes.label: Okroshka
dishes.origin: A cold summer soup of chopped salad poured over kvass just before serving, so the vegetables stay crunchy like cereal in milk.

dishes.label: Olivier salad
dishes.origin: A Moscow chef's secret dressing recipe was supposedly spied on by his sous-chef, who sold his own copy as Stolichny salad.

dishes.label: Onigiri
dishes.origin: Japan has carried these rice balls as portable food since ancient times; a 1980s packaging trick keeps the nori crisp until the wrapper is pulled.

dishes.label: Ossobuco
dishes.origin: Its name means bone with a hole, for the marrow in the veal shank; the older Milanese version had no tomatoes, only cinnamon, bay leaf and gremolada.

dishes.label: Oxtail soup
dishes.origin: Why 'ox' but 'beef'? After the Norman Conquest the lords ate 'beef' while English peasants got the 'ox' cuts, tails included.

dishes.label: Pabellón criollo
dishes.origin: Venezuela's national dish blends Native, Spanish and African traditions; plantain slices on the sides are jokingly called its guard rails.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Pabellón Criollo (Venezuelan Rice and Beans with Steak)

dishes.label: Pączki
dishes.origin: Poles eat them on Fat Thursday to use up lard, sugar and eggs before Lent; Hamtramck, Michigan, throws a Pączki Day parade.

dishes.label: Pad kra pao
dishes.origin: Thailand's go-to street lunch only took off after 1957; early cookbooks seasoned it with just fish sauce and palm sugar.

dishes.label: Pad Thai
dishes.origin: Invented in the 1930s-40s when Thailand's government pushed noodles over rice to build national identity; its name means 'Thai stir-fry'.

dishes.label: Paella
dishes.origin: Rice farmers by Valencia's Albufera lagoon cooked it over orange and pine wood; Valencians say only theirs is true paella.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Mastering the Art of Cooking Paellas

dishes.label: Pakora
dishes.origin: A 12th-century Indian cookbook already describes frying vegetables in gram-flour batter, and one older text even moulds the batter into fish shapes.

dishes.label: Pambazo
dishes.origin: Its name comes from pan basso, low-class bread from Mexico's viceregal days; in Veracruz tiny pambacitos stand in for canapés at parties.

dishes.label: Panang curry
dishes.origin: Its name may come from a Malay word for grilled, and an 1889 Thai cookbook already had a chicken version; the thick coconut sauce is milder than red curry.

dishes.label: Panettone
dishes.origin: Milan's tall Christmas bread is hung upside down to cool; legend says a baker named Tony made it to win a noble's daughter, and Peru now eats more than Italy.

dishes.label: Panipuri
dishes.origin: Nobody knows who invented it; in Delhi it's golgappa, in Kolkata phuchka, and manners say you eat each one whole in a single bite.

dishes.label: Panna cotta
dishes.origin: Its name means cooked cream, yet no Italian cookbook used it before the 1960s; Piedmont now lists it as a traditional product.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Panna Cotta with Red Fruit Sauce

dishes.label: Panzanella
dishes.origin: Before the 20th century it was a bread-and-onion salad; tomatoes only crashed the party later. Florentine traditionalists still frown on extras.

dishes.label: Pão de queijo
dishes.origin: Miners in Minas Gerais had no wheat, so cooks borrowed cassava starch from Indigenous people; grated cheese joined in around the 1800s.

dishes.label: Parmigiana
dishes.origin: Calabria, Campania, Apulia and Sicily all claim it, and a Naples recipe from 1837 first paired it with tomato.

dishes.label: Pašticada
dishes.origin: Dalmatia's festival beef braise has a 15th-century recipe from Dubrovnik, and a cousin called pastitsada turns up on the Greek island of Corfu.

dishes.label: Pastitsio
dishes.origin: Its name comes from Venetian pasticcio, but the Greek version with a thick béchamel crown was popularised by the chef Nikolaos Tselementes.

dishes.label: Pâté chinois
dishes.origin: Quebec's three-layer beef, corn and potato bake was voted a national dish in a Le Devoir poll, yet nobody agrees why it is called Chinese pie.

dishes.label: Pav bhaji
dishes.origin: Born as a fast lunch for Mumbai's textile mill workers; the bread is toasted on the griddle in so much butter it nearly soaks through.

dishes.label: Pavlova
dishes.origin: Named for the ballerina Anna Pavlova, it has sparked a century-long Australia-New Zealand row; neither side can prove it was theirs first.

dishes.label: Pelmeni
dishes.origin: Siberians once froze sacks of them outdoors in winter and carried them into the taiga as ready provisions.

dishes.label: Pemmican
dishes.origin: Fur traders and polar explorers swore by this Indigenous fat-and-dried-meat food, and a dispute over its export even sparked the 1814 Pemmican War.

dishes.label: Pho
dishes.origin: Noodle vendors in northern Vietnam sold it from shoulder poles around 1900; refugees later carried it worldwide, and Vietnam holds a Day of Pho.

dishes.label: Picadillo
dishes.origin: Its name means 'mince'; Cubans add olives and capers while Filipinos make a soupy version, and cooks argue endlessly over whether raisins belong.

dishes.label: Pierogi
dishes.origin: Poland's first printed cookbook already had a recipe in 1682, and Krakow's pierogi festival has served 30,000 in a day.

dishes.label: Pirozhki
dishes.origin: The name just means little pies; Volga Germans took versions to the US as runza, and Japan breads and fries them as piroshiki.

dishes.label: Po' boy
dishes.origin: Said to be named in 1929 when two ex-streetcar-conductor brothers handed free sandwiches to striking colleagues as another poor boy.

dishes.label: Poffertjes
dishes.origin: Dutch fairs sold these puffy yeast pancakes by 1746. Some say monks invented them, and Indonesia's kue cubit is a descendant.

dishes.label: Poke
dishes.origin: Hawaiian for 'to slice', it began as fishermen's trimmings eaten with sea salt and seaweed, then picked up soy sauce and sesame oil from Asian immigrants.

dishes.label: Porchetta
dishes.origin: Italian vendors sell it from white vans at fairs, and Minnesota's Iron Range spells it porketta.

dishes.label: Pork pie
dishes.origin: Melton Mowbray's pies won EU protection in 2008, and East Midlands families still eat them for breakfast at Christmas.

dishes.label: Pot-au-feu
dishes.origin: King Henry IV wanted every peasant to have a hen in the pot; one Perpignan pot-au-feu simmered nonstop for centuries.

dishes.label: Potato pancake
dishes.origin: Latkes are a Hanukkah staple; draniki are a national dish of Belarus, and in Poland a thick goulash-topped one is called brigand's.

dishes.label: Pozole
dishes.origin: Served on New Year's Eve across Mexico and New Mexico; the Aztecs were already cooking it for feasts in the 1500s.

dishes.label: Puff puff
dishes.origin: A fried-dough party snack from Nigeria; cousins are Ghana's bofrot, East Africa's mandazi and South Africa's vetkoek.

dishes.label: Pupusa
dishes.origin: El Salvador keeps a National Pupusa Day each November, timed to the corn harvest, and Honduras famously ceded the dish to its neighbour in trade talks.

dishes.label: Puran poli
dishes.origin: Its recipe shows up in a 12th-century Sanskrit encyclopedia, and Maharashtra makes it for Holi and Gudhi Padwa.

dishes.label: Puto
dishes.origin: Likely a cousin of south Indian puttu; in Bulacan the cheese-topped kind gets a cheeky local nickname and goes with dinuguan.

dishes.label: Quesabirria
dishes.origin: Tijuana taqueros added melted cheese to birria tacos around 2009; Instagram then made them a craze in Los Angeles. The tortilla gets dunked in the stew's fat.

dishes.label: Quiche
dishes.origin: Its name probably comes from a German word for cake; in the 1980s a satirical book, Real Men Don't Eat Quiche, made the farmhouse tart a snobbery symbol.

dishes.label: Quiche Lorraine
dishes.origin: Purists swear the real thing has no cheese; it was served in Lorraine on May Day, and the name may come from German Kuchen.

dishes.label: Raita
dishes.origin: Its name blends the Sanskrit words for black mustard seed and pungent, yet today's raitas mostly cool the palate.

dishes.label: Ramen
dishes.origin: Born in Yokohama's Chinatown as a cheap Chinese noodle soup, it was once called shina soba; instant ramen arrived in 1958.

dishes.label: Ratatouille
dishes.origin: A humble Provençal way to use up summer vegetables; its modern recipe only reached print around 1930, and tomatoes were once feared in France.

dishes.label: Red velvet cake
dishes.origin: New York's Waldorf-Astoria and Toronto's Eaton's both claim it; the red once came from cocoa reacting with buttermilk, before food dye took over.

dishes.label: Rendang
dishes.origin: Minangkabau travellers packed it as provisions because slow-cooked dry rendang keeps for weeks. Malaysia and Indonesia both claim it as a national dish.

dishes.label: Rice noodle roll
dishes.origin: A dim sum staple from Guangdong, rolled around shrimp or beef; in Guangzhou it was once called 'pull intestines' for how it is hand-pulled.

dishes.label: Risotto
dishes.origin: Legend says a glass painter who used saffron as a pigment slipped it into a wedding-feast rice dish in Milan, giving risotto its golden colour.

dishes.label: Rogan josh
dishes.origin: Mughal rulers carried it from Persia to cool Kashmir, and its red glow came from alkanet and chillies long before tomatoes joined in the West.

dishes.label: Ropa vieja
dishes.origin: The name means old clothes for its tattered strands of beef; it likely began as a Sephardic Shabbat stew in Spain and the Canary Islands.

dishes.label: Rugelach
dishes.origin: Its name echoes the Polish word for horn or corner; a legend ties it to croissants, but both crescents are far older than that story.

dishes.label: Sabich
dishes.origin: An Iraqi Jewish Sabbath breakfast became a sandwich in 1961 when a kiosk owner named Sabich fed hungry bus drivers; it took his name.

dishes.label: Sachertorte
dishes.origin: Invented in Vienna in 1832 for Prince Metternich, it sparked a decades-long court fight between the Hotel Sacher and the Demel bakery over who owned it.

dishes.label: Salade niçoise
dishes.origin: Nice's purists, led by an ex-mayor, ban cooked vegetables, and a chef posting a potato-and-bean version in 2016 sparked outrage.

dishes.label: Salchipapa
dishes.origin: Born as Lima street food, its name just squeezes 'sausage' and 'potato' together; Colombia and Bolivia have made it their own too.

dishes.label: Salisbury steak
dishes.origin: Named after Dr James Salisbury, a 19th-century American doctor who prescribed minced beef patties for digestive trouble; the name stuck by 1897.

dishes.label: Sambar
dishes.origin: One legend says a Maratha royal cook swapped kokum for tamarind in a lentil soup and named the result after a visiting prince.

dishes.label: Samosa
dishes.origin: Its name comes from a Persian word for triangular pastry, and a medieval Delhi poet already praised princes eating them.

dishes.label: Sancocho
dishes.origin: From the Spanish for 'to parboil'. Panama's version doubles as a hangover cure and a symbol of the country's mixed heritage.

dishes.label: Sarma
dishes.origin: An Ottoman wrap-and-roll classic; Romanians call it sarmale and call it their national dish, and a Lenten rice-only version is nicknamed 'liar's dolma'.

dishes.label: Satay
dishes.origin: Skewered grilled meat reached Java through Arab, Indian and Chinese traders; today it is a national dish of both Indonesia and Malaysia.

dishes.label: Sauerbraten
dishes.origin: Germans soak the roast for days in a vinegary marinade; legend says Julius Caesar or Charlemagne started it, and some Rhineland cooks add raisins.

dishes.label: Schnitzel
dishes.origin: By Austrian law a true Wiener schnitzel must be veal; make it with pork and it has to be called 'Wiener Art', or Viennese style.

dishes.label: Scouse
dishes.origin: Sailors' lobscouse gave Liverpudlians their nickname. Scousers argue over beef versus lamb, and a meatless 'blind scouse' also exists.

dishes.label: Scrapple
dishes.origin: Pennsylvania Dutch butchers made it to waste nothing, jokingly using everything but the oink, and Delaware throws an Apple Scrapple Festival for it.

dishes.label: Semla
dishes.origin: Sweden's Lent bun is blamed for a king's death in 1771: he reportedly ate fourteen after a huge dinner.

dishes.label: Shabu-shabu
dishes.origin: Named for the swish-swish sound of meat in the pot; Osaka's Suehiro trademarked the name in 1952.

dishes.label: Shakshuka
dishes.origin: Its name means 'mixture' in Arabic; Maghrebi Jews carried it to Israel in the 1950s, where it became a national breakfast.

dishes.label: Shashlik
dishes.origin: The word is Turkic for skewer, and it reached Moscow only in the late 1800s; by the 1920s it was a street-food staple across Russia.

dishes.label: Shawarma
dishes.origin: Shawarma's turning-spit trick came from Turkish doner, and Lebanese migrants carried it to Mexico, where it turned into tacos al pastor.

dishes.label: Shchi
dishes.origin: Cabbage soup has fed Russians since the 9th century; the old proverb says shchi and kasha are our food.

dishes.label: Shepherd's pie
dishes.origin: Called cottage pie since 1791; the French cousin hachis Parmentier honours the man who popularised the potato in France.

dishes.label: Shumai
dishes.origin: The name means 'sold on the side': tea houses served it as a sideline to tea, and Hohhot still sells it by the weight of the wrapper alone.

dishes.label: Sinigang
dishes.origin: The Philippines' tangy comfort soup; its name means 'stewed', and TasteAtlas crowned it the world's best soup in 2021.

dishes.label: Sisig
dishes.origin: Angeles City's Aling Lucing reinvented it in 1974 using pig heads left over from a nearby US air base; a yearly festival celebrates it.

dishes.label: Smørrebrød
dishes.origin: The name began as smør og brød, butter and bread; the Danes pile on toppings like herring, liver pate and egg, and the pile is eaten with a knife and fork.

dishes.label: Smyrna meatballs
dishes.origin: Greek refugees from Asia Minor carried these cumin-heavy oblong meatballs to Greece; the name means spicy little sausages.

dishes.label: Solyanka
dishes.origin: Its name once meant settler's soup; East Germans loved it, and Angela Merkel grew up on it. Russians swear it cures a hangover.

dishes.label: Songpyeon
dishes.origin: Korean families make these half-moon rice cakes for Chuseok and steam them on a bed of pine needles, which scents them.

dishes.label: Sopa de mondongo
dishes.origin: A tripe soup found from Argentina to the Philippines; Dominican cooks wash the tripe in lime first and finish it with a fiery fermented orange-juice sauce.

dishes.label: Sope
dishes.origin: A fried masa cake with pinched edges that act as a wall; in Oaxaca cooks sometimes top it with roasted grasshoppers.

dishes.label: Souvlaki
dishes.origin: Skewer grills date to Bronze Age Santorini; in Athens the skewer is called kalamaki, 'little reed', while in the north it is souvlaki.

dishes.label: Spring roll
dishes.place: China and across East and Southeast Asia
dishes.origin: Eaten at Spring Festival in China, where it began as a pancake of fresh spring vegetables; in the Netherlands it is a loempia.

dishes.label: Stamppot
dishes.origin: Dutch legend ties hutspot to the 1574 Siege of Leiden, though stamppot with raw leafy greens only dates to about 1940.

dishes.label: Stargazy Pie
dishes.origin: Baked for Tom Bawcock's Eve in Mousehole, with fish heads poking through the crust to gaze at the stars and prove the catch is inside.

dishes.label: Steak and kidney pie
dishes.origin: Mrs Beeton printed the first steak-and-kidney recipe in 1859, though as a pudding; the pie only caught up later.

dishes.label: Steak Tartare
dishes.origin: Once called steak a l'Americaine; the 'tartare' came from tartar sauce, and a tale of Tatar horsemen tenderising raw meat under saddles.

dishes.label: Sticky toffee pudding
dishes.origin: A Lake District hotel made it famous in the 1970s, and a village shop in Cartmel later sold a take-home version that reached supermarkets by the late 1990s.

dishes.label: Stollen
dishes.origin: Medieval Saxon bakers wrote to the Pope for permission to use butter, and the 1490 Butter Letter finally allowed it, for a fee.

dishes.label: Strudel
dishes.origin: Purists say the dough must be pulled so thin you could read a newspaper through it; it likely descends from Hungarian rétes, itself kin to baklava.

dishes.label: Succotash
dishes.origin: Its name comes from a Narragansett word for broken corn kernels; Depression-era cooks loved how cheap it was.

dishes.label: Sukiyaki
dishes.origin: Meiji-era cooks simmer thin beef at the table; each bite gets dunked in raw beaten egg, and Kantō folk adopted Kansai style after 1923.

dishes.label: Summer roll
dishes.origin: Never fried: in the south it is gỏi cuốn, in the north nem cuốn, and abroad it is sold as a summer, salad or fresh spring roll.

dishes.label: Sundubu-jjigae
dishes.origin: A Joseon official is said to have set the first sundubu with sea water; LA's Koreatown opened the first US sundubu restaurant in 1986.

dishes.label: Svíčková
dishes.origin: The name means tenderloin, yet it uses beef topside. Often mistranslated 'candle sauce', it comes with a creamy root-vegetable sauce.

dishes.label: Syrniki
dishes.origin: Fried curd-cheese pancakes shared by Ukraine, Russia and Belarus; a Russian name for them, tvorozhniki, comes from the curd, tvorog.

dishes.label: Tabbouleh
dishes.origin: Lebanon holds a National Tabbouleh Day each July, and the Levantine original has far more parsley than grain.

dishes.label: Taco al pastor
dishes.origin: Lebanese immigrants brought shawarma to Puebla and swapped lamb for pork, then added chilies and pineapple, shaved from a spinning trompo.

dishes.label: Tafelspitz
dishes.origin: Emperor Franz Joseph ate boiled beef so often that it became Vienna's signature; the name means 'top of the table'.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Table Point Boiled Beef and Vegetables (Tafelspitz)

dishes.label: Tagine
dishes.origin: The stew is named after its cone-lidded clay pot, which traps steam and so needs hardly any water; the cone shape began in Tafraout.

dishes.label: Takoyaki
dishes.origin: A street vendor named Tomekichi Endo is credited with creating these octopus balls in Osaka in 1935 by mixing two older snacks.

dishes.label: Tamagoyaki
dishes.origin: Edo townsfolk first steamed a fluffy broth-and-egg dish; by the 1960s Japanese kids ranked it beside the Giants and a sumo star.

dishes.label: Tamale
dishes.origin: Aztec women stayed up for days cooking tamales before a wedding, and the Maya painted tamales on pots over 1,200 years ago.

dishes.label: Tangyuan
dishes.origin: Round rice balls in sweet soup eaten at the Lantern Festival; their name sounds like 'reunion', which is why families serve them together.

dishes.label: Tarte flambée
dishes.origin: Alsatian farmers used it to test their wood ovens: when the fire peaked, the thin dough baked in one or two minutes.

dishes.label: Tarte Tatin
dishes.origin: Said to be born of a mistake at a hotel run by the Tatin sisters in the 1880s, though historians suspect it was a branded local tart.

dishes.label: Tempura
dishes.origin: Portuguese missionaries in Nagasaki brought the batter-frying idea; its name may come from the Latin word for the fasting days, tempora.

dishes.label: Red curry
dishes.origin: Its fiery colour comes from dried spur chillies pounded in a mortar, and the paste itself seasons other Thai dishes like fish cakes and Chiang Mai sausage.

dishes.label: Thieboudienne
dishes.origin: Born in Saint-Louis in the 1800s, Senegal's national dish gave jollof rice its family tree. Its Wolof name simply means rice and fish.

dishes.label: Tiramisu
dishes.origin: Nobody agrees who made it first, but a Treviso restaurant put it on its menu in 1972, and its name means 'pick me up'.

dishes.label: Tlayuda
dishes.origin: A dinner-plate-sized Oaxacan tortilla, toasted on a clay comal and kept in a palm basket until leathery-crisp; the toppings have no strict rules.

dishes.label: Toad in the hole
dishes.origin: It began as a cheap way to stretch scraps of meat in batter, and despite the name no recipe has ever used a toad; the first versions used pigeon or steak.

dishes.label: Tom kha kai
dishes.origin: First written down around 1890 as a duck soup with young galangal; chicken took over later, and 'kha' is the Thai word for galangal.

dishes.label: Tom yum
dishes.origin: Its name means 'boiled mixed'; the creamy version with milk only arrived in the 1980s, while the clear soup is the older style.

dishes.label: Tonkatsu
dishes.origin: Invented around 1899 at Tokyo's Rengatei restaurant from a French veal cutlet; a smaller sandwich version was made so geishas would not smudge their lipstick.

dishes.label: Tonkotsu ramen
dishes.origin: Born at a Kurume street stall in 1937, its milky broth is said to have come from a pot that was accidentally boiled too long.

dishes.label: Tostada
dishes.origin: A stale tortilla fried crisp becomes a tostada; Oaxaca's pizza-sized version, the tlayuda, is sometimes topped with fried grasshoppers.

dishes.label: Tourtière
dishes.origin: Quebec's Christmas Eve meat pie. Its name comes from the baking dish, not from the passenger pigeon (tourte) of popular legend.

dishes.label: Trifle
dishes.origin: In 2022 a lemon Swiss roll and amaretti trifle won the Platinum Pudding contest for the Queen's jubilee. The name once meant a thick cream, not a layered cake.

dishes.label: Tteokbokki
dishes.origin: The royal court once ate it in soy sauce; the red chili version appeared in 1953 when a cook dropped rice cake into jajangmyeon.

dishes.label: Turducken
dishes.origin: Chef Paul Prudhomme trademarked it in 1986, and John Madden made it a Thanksgiving football legend by carving one live in the broadcast booth.

dishes.label: Turkish delight
dishes.origin: Its Turkish name, lokum, comes from an Arabic phrase meaning 'comfort of the throat'; Cyprus holds protected status for its own version.

dishes.label: Turtle soup
dishes.origin: London's Lord Mayor's banquet served it every year from 1761 to 1825; calf's-head 'mock turtle' took over once the real thing grew pricey.

dishes.label: Umm Ali
dishes.origin: Egypt's national dessert, named for 'Ali's mother'; legend says a sultan's wife ordered it in celebration, though the first real recipe is 19th century.

source.cookbook: Cookbook:Puff Pastry with Nuts and Whipped Cream (Om Ali)

dishes.label: Upma
dishes.origin: Its many names all echo uppu, the Dravidian word for salt; in Kerala it is often paired with a mashed banana.

dishes.label: Vichyssoise
dishes.place: New York City (by a French chef)
dishes.origin: Named after a French spa town yet invented at New York's Ritz-Carlton by Louis Diat, who served it chilled to cool down a hot summer's day.

dishes.label: Vindaloo
dishes.origin: It began as Portuguese pork marinated in wine and garlic; Goan cooks swapped in palm vinegar and spice, and Britain made it a fiery pub-closing dare.

dishes.label: Vitello tonnato
dishes.origin: A Piedmont summer classic of cold veal under tuna mayonnaise; Argentines, Uruguayans and Paraguayans serve it at Christmas as vitel toné.

dishes.label: Waldorf salad
dishes.origin: Created for a charity ball at New York's Waldorf-Astoria in 1896 by its maitre d'; the first version had no walnuts.

dishes.label: Welsh cake
dishes.origin: Miners in the South Wales coalfield carried these griddle-cooked cakes underground in their food boxes, and Wales eats them on St David's Day.

dishes.label: Welsh rarebit
dishes.origin: Its first recorded name, in 1725, was 'Welsh rabbit', a joke since it holds no rabbit; 'rarebit' came later and purists have grumbled ever since.

dishes.label: Wonton
dishes.origin: Cantonese 'cloud swallow' wontons float like little clouds in the broth. Sichuan folds them as 'crossed arms' and serves them in red chili oil.

dishes.label: Xiaolongbao
dishes.origin: The soup inside is jellied meat aspic wrapped in with the filling, which melts into broth when steamed; the style grew out of Kaifeng's soup-filled buns.

dishes.label: Yakisoba
dishes.origin: Despite the name, it uses wheat noodles, not buckwheat soba; it began at 1920s Tokyo street stalls as a cheap swap for flour in okonomiyaki-style snacks.

dishes.label: Yakitori
dishes.origin: 'Grilled bird' on a stick, best over binchotan charcoal, and sold from street carts, izakaya, even vacuum packs and cans since 1970.

dishes.label: Yangzhou fried rice
dishes.origin: Named for Yangzhou, though it began elsewhere; a 2015 world-record attempt there was disqualified when part of the batch went to pigs.

dishes.label: Yellow curry
dishes.origin: Thai yellow curry is the mildest of the big three, and the Western curry powder sold under the same name is a different blend.

dishes.label: Yorkshire pudding
dishes.origin: It started as a thrifty first course to dull appetites before the costly roast meat, and chemists once insisted a real one must stand four inches tall.

dishes.label: Zapiekanka
dishes.origin: A 1970s Polish street food built on baguettes licensed from France; the stands at Kraków's Plac Nowy became cult favourites.

dishes.label: Zhajiangmian
dishes.origin: A tale says Empress Dowager Cixi tasted it on the run in Xi'an in 1900 and took its noodle chef home; Korea's jajangmyeon is its cousin.

dishes.label: Zongzi
dishes.origin: Eaten for Dragon Boat Festival; legend says people threw rice into the river to keep fish from the drowned poet Qu Yuan.
